column3: Fourier epicycles. A 128x128 black void where a chain of rotating circles, each arm spinning at its own integer frequency (the Fourier series of a closed curve, as in 3Blue1Brown's drawing machines), traces the time with a pen of light. Each numeral is one closed path, so each has its own set of coefficients; the arms are drawn as fine glowing rings and spokes, the pen leaves a trail that fades along its length, so the numeral is always being redrawn and never static. Design numeral paths that are beautiful as single closed loops (a calligraphic, monoline 'one stroke' figure set) and that a few dozen terms can draw crisply on this grid; the four digits could be four machines, or one machine visiting all four, or hours big and minutes smaller: compose it, don't default to 2x2. Always alive: the circles turn at 60 fps, the trail shimmers, the pen sparks. Minute turn: the coefficients of the old digit interpolate to the new one (smoothly, term by term, high frequencies first or last: design it), so the drawn path morphs continuously from one numeral to the next; make sure the in-between never reads as a third numeral (fade the trail through the morph if needed). Hour: the machine unfolds into its full set of spinning circles, a grand flourish (a spiral, a rose), then condenses back. Mathematics as light.

Ice rink at night. The 128x64 board is a floodlit outdoor ice rink seen from above (rounded corners, boards with ads, the centre circle and blue lines): the 2:1 shape is a rink. The time is carved into the ice: skaters (bold, readable from above: scarves, swinging arms, real skating gait with gliding strides and crossovers) glide along the numerals' paths and their blades cut bright white grooves into the dark polished ice, so the numerals are made of skate tracks (design an ice-script letterform: carved double lines with spray at the turns, figure-skating flourishes). Always alive: skaters circle and leave fresh scratches, the floodlights' reflections slide on the ice, snow falls and settles, breath puffs. Minute turn: an ice resurfacer (Zamboni) drives a lap over the changing digit, its wide wet blade erasing the grooves to a mirror-black sheen that steams, and a figure skater then carves the new numeral in one performance (spins and a jump leave a spray). Hour: the rink lights go to a show (spotlights, a pair skating), the whole surface is resurfaced and the time carved again, staying readable. Mirror ice on black GOB is the wow.

Shadow-puppet theatre (皮影戏). The 128x64 board is the lit cloth screen of a Chinese shadow-play stage: a warm flickering lamp behind it, translucent dyed-leather puppets pressed against the cloth so they show in rich transparent colour (red, green, ochre, black) with fine pierced patterns, the control rods visible as thin dark lines. The time is told by the puppets: the four numerals are themselves carved leather puppets (jointed at the strokes' joints, with pierced openwork patterns, held up on rods), or held as placards by the characters: design a carved-leather numeral set with openwork that still reads boldly. Always alive: the lamp flickers and the shadows breathe, puppets bob on their rods, limbs swing on their joints with real pendulum physics, a soft halo where a puppet lifts off the cloth and blurs. Minute turn: a puppet character (a general, a monkey king, a dancer) strides on, fights or dances with the changing numeral puppet, which tumbles away limb by limb, and the new numeral is swung onto the screen and jointed together. Hour: a full scene with drums and cymbals (a dragon, a battle), the time stays readable. Warm light through coloured leather.

Dandelion clock. A 64x128 tall meadow at the real time of day: a dandelion stem rises from the grass, and the time is in the seed heads ('dandelion clock', the folk game of telling the hour by blowing seeds). The numerals are made of dandelion seeds: each seed a pappus (a fine white parachute on a thin stalk), packed along the numeral's strokes like a seed head shaped into a figure (design the seed-numeral; bold enough to read at 2 m: many seeds, glowing against the sky). Always alive: a breeze sways the stems, seeds tremble, a few break loose and drift up the tall board with real light-parachute flight (tumbling, slow rise and fall in the wind), sunlight or moonlight catches them, insects drift. Minute turn: a gust strips the changing digit's seeds, which float away up the tower in a beautiful cloud, and new seeds grow back from the bare receptacle and fluff out into the new numeral. Hour: the whole meadow lets go in a great drift of seeds that fills the sky, and the time reforms. Soft, airy, physical. Time of day drives the palette (dawn gold, day blue, dusk pink, night silver).

Cinema projector. A 192x64 dark cinema in side view: at the left a 35 mm projector with two spinning reels, the film looping through the gate, a flickering lamp house; its beam crosses the room in a cone through drifting dust and cigarette smoke (lit volumetrically, dust motes glittering), and lands on a screen that fills the right two-thirds. The time is the film: shown on the screen as classic film-leader countdown numerals (the 'Academy leader' with the sweeping circle hand, cross-hairs, scratches, dust, gate weave, flicker at 24 fps) designed for this grid, or the time projected as the film's title card; the frame visibly matches what passes through the gate. Always alive: reels turn, film flutters, the beam shimmers with dust, a silhouette in the front row shifts, scratches and gate weave on the screen. Minute turn: a changeover: the leader counts down on the changing numeral (its sweep hand circles), a cue dot flashes in the corner, the film runs out and flaps, the second projector's beam takes over with the new numeral fading in through a burn-in. Hour: an intermission: the house lights rise, curtains close and reopen, a newsreel title for the hour. Warm beam on black.

Mahjong table. A 256x64 close-up of a mahjong game on green baize: a player's rack of tiles along the banner, ivory-and-green tiles in real 3D (rounded edges, the green back, the carved and painted faces, a highlight). The time is four tiles in the hand, stood out from the rest: the digits are mahjong numerals (the characters suit 一 二 三 四 五 六 七 八 九 above 萬, with the white dragon 白板, the blank tile, as zero), or the circles/bamboo suits where counting reads well: choose what reads fastest at 2 m, and design the carved tile faces for this grid with real lacquer colours (red, green, blue-black). Other tiles in the hand and the discards on the table are dimmer and clearly secondary. Always alive: hands reach in and shuffle, tiles click and settle with a bounce, dice roll, the wall of tiles shimmers in lamp light, steam from a cup of tea. Minute turn: draw and discard: a tile is drawn from the wall, slid across, flipped face up (real 3D rotation), and swapped into the changing slot while the old tile is discarded to the table with a click. Hour: a winning hand is declared, the whole rack is pushed down face up with a clatter (the time stays readable), then the tiles are shuffled with a swirl and a new hand is built. Tactile, clicky, cultural.

Astronomical clock tower. A 64x192 cutaway of Su Song's 11th-century water-driven clock tower (水运仪象台, Kaifeng): an armillary sphere on the roof platform, a celestial globe turning in the middle storey, and below a five-tier wooden pagoda of little doors where puppet figures appear holding time placards, all driven by a great water wheel with scoops at the base, its escapement tripping one scoop at a time. The time is announced by the puppets: figures in Song dress step out of the doors with placards bearing the numerals (design a carved, lacquered placard numeral set: gold on red, or black on cream, bold), bells and drums struck by other figures. Always alive: water pours into the scoops, the wheel ticks round by the escapement in jerky physical steps, the globe turns, the sphere's rings catch the light, lanterns glow. Minute turn: the escapement trips, gears visibly drive a puppet out, the changing digit's figure bows and withdraws, the next steps out with the new placard. Hour: drums and bells, all tiers' doors open in sequence, a procession of figures; the time stays readable. Warm lacquer, gold, bronze and water.

Tangram. Five panels in a plus are a tangram set on a dark lacquered table: in each of the four arms the seven classic pieces (two large triangles, a medium triangle, two small triangles, a square, a parallelogram) are arranged into a numeral (tangram digits are a real puzzle tradition: design ten readable ones, all from the same seven pieces, upright in every arm), and the centre panel is the box they live in. The pieces are real objects: lacquered wood or translucent coloured glass in a restrained palette (one material per time unit), with bevels, a highlight, a soft shadow, a fine gap between pieces. Always alive: pieces breathe and shimmer, a lamp's reflection glides over them, a piece occasionally nudges itself into a more exact place. Minute turn: the changing arm's seven pieces lift, glide and rotate (rigid motions, eased, with a little hover and shadow) into the new numeral's arrangement, rearranging rather than fading (every piece is always present: never a different digit on the way: a muddle is fine). Hour: all 28 pieces fly into the centre box and assemble the classic square, then a figure (a cat, a crane, a running man), then fly back out to the time. Geometric, satisfying, physical.

Pancake art. Three panels in an L: the long bottom arm is a hot griddle seen from slightly above, the tall left arm is the cook's station rising above it (the squeeze bottle in a hand, a hood with steam and heat shimmer rising up the column, utensils hanging). The time is pancake art: the numerals are drawn in batter from a squeeze bottle, and batter browns with time on the griddle, so the lines drawn first are darker (the real pancake-art trick): the numerals' shading literally records the order they were drawn (design a piped-batter numeral set with thick-to-thin flow and a browned outline). Always alive: bubbles rise and pop in the batter, butter sizzles and shimmers, steam rises up the tall arm, the edges crisp. Minute turn: the bottle draws the new numeral's lines beside the old (or a spatula slides under the old pancake and flips it in real 3D, showing its browned face), the old one is lifted away onto a plate up the tall arm, and the fill batter floods the new outline. Hour: a stack of pancakes grows in the tall arm, syrup pours down it, the hour numeral is the pancake on top. Warm, appetising, physical.

Digital water curtain. A 128x192 portrait of a graphical waterfall (the installations where a row of valves releases droplets that fall as printed letters): a lit sheet of falling water, back-lit or lit from below in a designed colour, with a black pool and splashes at the bottom. The time is printed in falling water: the valves release the numerals as patterns of drops that fall under real gravity (accelerating, so letters stretch slightly as they fall: design numerals that read while stretched, pre-squashed at the top), and the print repeats, so at any moment at least one full copy of the time is in view and readable (or the curtain pauses and holds the time as a hovering word, then lets it fall). Design a 'droplet type' set: strokes made of fat glistening drops with highlights. Always alive: drops fall at 60 fps, each glints, splashes and ripples in the pool, mist rises, the light colour drifts slowly. Minute turn: the next print carries the new numeral, the old one falls away into the pool, and the switch must never show a wrong time (the old and new copies in view must not be confused: mark the newest copy, or clear the curtain between). Hour: the whole curtain performs (a wave, a spiral, a curtain-wide pattern) before printing the new time. The tall shape is the fall.

Sliding puzzle. Nine panels, 3 by 3, are a giant sliding tile puzzle (the 8-puzzle): each panel is one tile, and one tile is always the empty space (drawn as a dark recessed tray with a felt floor, so the panel's lights are not wasted: it shows depth and shadow). The tiles carry one picture that the time is part of: a single 192x192 illustration (your theme: a landscape, a poster, a mosaic) with the time painted across it in big numerals, so when the tiles are in order the time reads, and scrambled tiles don't. Real tile objects: bevelled edges, a gloss highlight, a shadow cast into the empty slot, a slight click as they seat. Always alive: tiles jiggle in their slots, the gloss moves, the picture itself is alive (water, clouds, lights). Minute turn: the puzzle slides: a sequence of tile moves (smooth, eased, one tile at a time, the empty space travelling) carries the changing digit's tiles out and brings new tiles whose painted numeral is the new digit into place; design it so the time is never wrong in between (the digit area may be scrambled, never a wrong number). Hour: the whole puzzle scrambles in a flurry and solves itself back, the classic solution rhythm, then the empty tile moves to a new home. The 3x3 grid of panels is the puzzle.

Kintsugi. The 64x64 panel is a dark ceramic bowl seen from above (deep black-blue glaze with a subtle crackle and a speckled foot ring), lit by a soft window light. The time is the gold: the numerals are kintsugi seams (cracks mended with gold lacquer), irregular, branching like real fractures, glinting where the light catches them; design fracture-numerals that read clearly as digits yet look like genuine break lines (jagged micro-steps, tapering ends, small gold-dust spots). Always alive: the window light shifts and a glint travels along the gold seams, the glaze shimmers, a faint reflection of a branch outside moves across the bowl. Minute turn: a crack runs: a fine hairline races across the glaze along the new numeral (with a tiny lift of the shards and a sound-like flash), the old gold seam fades back into the glaze as if healed, and liquid gold flows into the new crack from one end to the other, filling it with a bright meniscus that cools to gold. Hour: the whole bowl breaks into pieces that lift and hang apart (real 3D shards, the time still readable as gaps or gold edges), then reassemble with all seams flowing gold. Quiet, precious, beautiful.
